description:
A major geopolitical crisis is unfolding around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the most critical shipping routes in the world for oil and gas.

The waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf to global markets, is responsible for transporting a large portion of the world's energy supply. Rising tensions between Iran and the United States have now placed this strategic route at the center of a growing global crisis.

Donald Trump has called on other countries to help reopen the shipping lane, warning that disruptions could impact energy markets worldwide. However, Iranian officials say several countries have already contacted Tehran to negotiate safe passage for their ships.

Reports suggest European governments such as France and Italy may be in discussions with Iran to ensure their vessels can continue passing safely through the strait.

title: Strait of Hormuz Crisis: Iran Controls Global Oil Route

According to Marwan Bishara, the conflict could expand beyond Iran and Israel and potentially affect areas like Yemen and the Red Sea, which would have major consequences for global trade, energy supply, and regional stability.

The war is already affecting shipping routes, global energy distribution, and economic activity. Disruptions near the Strait of Hormuz could have a significant impact on oil markets and international shipping.

description:
Fuel prices across Europe have surged by up to 20 per cent since the war in Iran disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly a fifth of global supply. The sharp rise has triggered a wave of cross-border "fuel tourism", with drivers travelling from high-tax countries such as the Netherlands – where diesel now costs nearly three US dollars per litre – to neighbouring Belgium and Germany in search of savings. 
Many motorists are filling jerrycans in their boots despite safety warnings, while governments resist calls to cut fuel duties.

Al Jazeera's Step Vaessen reports from the Dutch-Belgian border.

description:

Organisers were confined to a fixed location on the South Bank of the River Thames, with police citing public order concerns and the risk of clashes with counter-protesters. For nearly 40 years the event has been allowed to march through the streets, but heightened tensions over the war in Gaza and the conflict involving Iran prompted authorities to enforce a static protest. Police warned demonstrators against displaying support for proscribed groups or using language that could be interpreted as inciting violence.

Al Jazeera's Rob McBride reports from London.

Salman Shaikh, founder of the Shaikh Group and former UN official, told Al Jazeera this is "the wrong war at the wrong moment without the right planning," noting Iran is fighting an existential, nationalist battle with a higher pain threshold while the US measures every soldier lost. Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University in Qatar said Tehran has demonstrated it can deal pain by keeping the Strait closed, forcing Gulf states to reconsider reliance on Washington.

He noted President Trump sounds "exceedingly desperate" and is escalating, but the longer the war continues, the costlier and riskier it becomes for both sides without bringing them closer to their goals. A growing number of fishermen are disappearing off the coast of Ecuador as the country faces an unprecedented security crisis.
In Ecuador’s Manabí Province, at least 80 fishermen have gone missing over the past year. Local authorities and fishing communities believe many of them may have fallen victim to criminal groups operating at sea, often referred to as “pirates.”

These attacks are part of a wider surge in violence across Ecuador. The country has seen a dramatic rise in organized crime linked to drug trafficking networks and powerful criminal gangs.

According to official figures, Ecuador recorded more than 9,000 murders last year, making it the most violent country per capita in Latin America. The wave of violence has affected cities, prisons, and now even coastal waters where fishermen rely on the ocean for their livelihoods.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
A drone strike has hit a key oil refinery in northern Iraq, sparking a fire and forcing officials to halt operations while the damage is assessed.

Authorities from Iraq’s Ministry of Natural Resources confirmed that the attack targeted the Lenaz refinery located in the Kurdistan region. The refinery plays an important role in distributing oil across northern Iraq, making the strike a significant concern for the region’s energy infrastructure.

Although the full extent of the damage is still being evaluated, officials say even limited disruption could impact fuel distribution and the regional economy. Oil production and export remain the backbone of the Kurdistan region’s economy.

The attack comes amid a growing wave of strikes across Iraq. Armed groups have recently targeted US bases, diplomatic facilities, and other strategic locations throughout the country.

The US embassy compound in Baghdad was also hit by missiles earlier the same day, damaging part of its air defense system.
